opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, because on the surface it sounds a little backwards. Usually you identify the problem first and then go find the tool. But with AI, I've found that approach actually slows you down.

The reason is that most people don't know what AI can do for them until they've spent real time with it. If you wait for someone to come up with the perfect use case before they start, they never start. They sit on the sidelines, they read about it, they form opinions, but they don't build intuition. And intuition only comes from use. So the mandate is really about getting people's hands dirty. Use it for writing an email, summarizing a spec, debugging a piece of code, preparing for a customer meeting, whatever. Once you've done that fifty or a hundred times, you start to see where it's genuinely useful and where it falls flat. That's when the real use cases show up, and they come from the people closest to the work, not from some top-down plan I could write.

There's also a more personal reason for us at d-Matrix. We build silicon for AI inference. Our whole thesis is that inference is going to be everywhere, that it's going to be the dominant workload, and that cost, latency and energy efficiency are going to matter enormously. It would be strange for us to say that to the world and not live it ourselves. If our engineers, our sales team, our operations people are all heavy users, they understand the workload at a gut level. They feel what it's like when a model is slow, when a response takes too long, when the interaction breaks down. That empathy for the end user makes us better at building the product.

And frankly, it's a competitive issue. The companies that figure out how to make every employee more productive with AI are going to move faster than the ones that don't. A startup like ours can't afford to move slowly. So I'd rather everybody start now, make some mistakes, learn what works, and then we compound from there. The "what" will come. The habit has to come first.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people often discover useful AI applications only after using it repeatedly, and that starting before identifying a use case lets real use cases emerge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short version is: you don't learn what a tool is good for by reading about it. You learn by picking it up and using it badly for a while.

When we made that call internally, a lot of people pushed back and said, look, tell me the use case first, and then I'll adopt it. And my answer was, that's backwards. If I could tell you the use case, I wouldn't need you to go discover it. The whole point is that the people closest to the work, the chip designers, the compiler folks, the people in finance, in recruiting, they are the ones who are going to find where these models actually help, and where they fall flat. I can't dictate that from the top.

The other piece is a little more personal to what we do. We're building the hardware that runs inference. If we're asking the world to bet on a future where AI is woven into everything, and we ourselves are not living in that future every day, then we don't really understand our own customer. Our engineers need to feel the latency, feel where the model gets things wrong, feel what it's like to wait on a slow response. That intuition shows up in the product.

And honestly, there's a cultural element. These tools change fast. If you wait until there's a clean ROI case, you're always six months behind the people who just started experimenting. I'd rather have a company full of people who have already burned their fingers a bit and know what's real, than a company waiting for permission.

So the mandate is really just: use it. Use it on your real work. Tell us what happened. The use cases come after.

r001.rationale: The response says employees should use AI before knowing the use case, because the people closest to the work will discover where it helps through experimentation.

astra-6.text:
Because you don’t really understand what AI can do for you until you start using it. If you wait until you have the perfect use case, you may never get started. So I want everyone to experiment, whether they’re in engineering, finance, sales, or HR. Take something you do every day and see whether AI can help.

The point isn’t to use AI just to say we’re using AI. It’s to build that familiarity so people can recognize opportunities in their own work. Some things won’t work, and that’s fine. But once you find something that saves you time or helps you think through a problem, you start asking, “What else could I do with this?” That’s the habit I want us to develop.

r001.rationale: The response says employees should experiment with AI before they have a perfect use case, so they can recognize opportunities in their own work.

sol-6.1.text: Because you have to get your hands on it to understand what it can do. If you wait until you have the perfect use case, you may never get started. So I tell everyone: use AI, experiment with it, and see where it helps you in your work. As you get comfortable, you start recognizing opportunities you wouldn’t have seen otherwise. And for us, building technology for AI, that firsthand experience is especially valuable. We should understand how people use these tools, where they work well, and where the friction is.
